newsitem.title: USA: Weather behind shorter US work week--Labor's Hamel. [CORRECTED 15:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Weather behind shorter US work week--Labor's Hamel. [CORRECTED 15:00 GMT]

text.p: A slight decline last month in the average number of hours in the U.S. workweek was due mainly to harsh winter weather and the trend for hours worked as well as hourly earnings is upward, Department of Labor economist Harvey Hamel said Friday.

The Labor Department reported that the average workweek fell to 34.1 hours last month, from 34.8 hours in December (corrects workweek figures), while average hourly earnings rose by one cent to $12.06.
Hamel said extreme cold weather throughout the country during the survey period contributed to the drop in the number of hours worked.
On earnings, Hamel said it was normal to see month-to-month differences in the level of gains and that a small rise after several strong increases in a row was not unusual.
"Over the year earnings increases have been accelerating since 1993 and 1994," he said. Hamel said he saw the trend in hours worked and hourly earnings still moving upward.
Seasonal adjustment factors may have exaggerated jobs gains in the help supply industry and in local education.
"That would tone down the service increase a bit," he said. But he added that he did not think those factors changed the overall employment picture for January.
